kurz: How large the reserve for emergencies needs to be, where it should be kept, why it does not belong in the portfolio and what it costs.

bloecke.md:
The over-indebtedness statistics of the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) name the most common triggers for 2025 as illness, addiction and accident (18.2%), unemployment (16.8%), poor household management (11.7%) and separation, divorce or death (11.1%). Three of the four largest items are events that affect income rather than spending behaviour. Over-indebtedness therefore rarely begins with an overly expensive purchase such as a television. Usually it starts with an unplanned gap in income and no reserve to bridge it.

This is what the emergency fund is for. Unlike an investment, it is not designed to generate a return. It is meant to prevent a household in an emergency from being forced to sell securities at the wrong time, use its arranged overdraft, buy on instalments or accept a job only because the rent is due in three weeks. Its benefit is measured by the costs it prevents; the interest is secondary.
The size of the emergency fund is measured against the expenses that continue even when no income comes in any more. Net income and the monthly budget are not the right basis for this.

## Essential and non-essential expenses

The relevant items are rent, energy, communication, insurance premiums, groceries, transport, medical co-payments and maintenance obligations. Not included are the monthly savings amount, holiday savings, restaurant visits and cancellable subscriptions, because without income nobody saves or goes travelling. The most common calculation error concerns the savings amount. It appears on the account statement like an expense, but in an emergency it is the first thing to be suspended.

bloecke.titel: Expenses of an example household in an emergency
zeilen: Transport (season ticket or fixed car costs)

bloecke.md: The basis of calculation for this household is €1,840, not €2,600. Three months come to €5,520, six months to €11,040. A household that instead puts aside six full monthly budgets ties up €15,600. That is around €4,560 more, which could be invested differently over decades without any measurable increase in security.

## Number of months

The range of three to six months is a guideline. It follows from how likely a loss of income is and how long it lasts. Where a household falls within this range depends on four points: the number of incomes, how quickly your own qualifications are in demand again on the labour market, the share of fixed costs and the possibility of cutting them at short notice, and the benefits of the social security system.

For employees with statutory health insurance, these benefits can be stated precisely. In the event of illness, the employer continues to pay full wages for six weeks. After that, the health insurance fund pays sickness benefit (Krankengeld) for a maximum of 72 weeks within three years (Section 48 SGB V, Social Code Book V on health insurance). However, it amounts to only around 70% of gross pay and at most 90% of net pay. One-off payments such as a Christmas bonus from the twelve months before the start of the incapacity for work are included on a pro rata basis (Section 47 SGB V). For employees, illness therefore means a cut in income rather than a loss of it. Unemployment puts greater strain on liquidity, because weeks can pass between dismissal, application and the first payment, and there is no telling how long the job search will take.

bloecke.titel: Target size by life situation, in months of essential expenses
zeilen: Two incomes rarely stop at the same time, and the remaining one is enough in the short term.
A loss affects the whole household, and the share of fixed costs is high and hard to reduce.
Probation, fixed-term contract, industry in transition
Protection against dismissal does not apply in the first six months, and the job search takes longer.
Home ownership with an outstanding loan
The loan's annuity payments continue, plus maintenance that cannot be postponed.
No continued pay during illness, as a rule no unemployment benefit (Arbeitslosengeld I), fluctuating incoming payments.
Receiving a pension, no earned income
Income is stable. The reserve covers repairs and health costs, not a loss of income.

bloecke.md: VAT, income tax prepayments and possible additional payments may sit in your own account, but they belong to the tax office. If this money is mixed with the reserve, the buffer is used up after the next tax assessment notice. The tax reserve and the reserve therefore belong in separate accounts, and only the reserve counts as the emergency fund.

## Building up the reserve

A reserve of eleven thousand euros has to be saved up over a long period. At €300 a month, building it takes just over three years. During this time many people give up or use the money for other purposes. The reserve is therefore built up in stages. A first stage of around €1,000 covers a typical one-off expense (repair, dental work, rental deposit, lawyer) and can be reached within a few months. Only the second stage is enough for a loss of income, and the third reaches the target size.

bloecke.md:
## Where to keep the reserve

The place for the reserve must meet three requirements. The amount must not fluctuate in nominal terms, it must be in the current account within a few working days, and it must not be spent by accident. An [[instant-access savings account]] meets all three. A fixed-term deposit fails the second requirement, the current account the third and the securities account the first.

Balances in current accounts, instant-access savings accounts and fixed-term deposits are protected throughout the EU by statutory [[deposit protection]] up to €100,000 per customer and bank. Many German institutions also belong to voluntary protection schemes. A reserve of the usual size stays well below this limit. The limit only becomes relevant if the same bank also holds a down payment for a property or a severance payment, because all of a customer's balances at one bank are added together.

The ECB deposit facility rate stood at 2.50% on 16 September 2026. Instant-access rates for existing customers are based on it and are usually lower. Advertised top offers of 4% and more are almost always promotions for new customers with three to six months of guaranteed interest. On €12,000, half a percentage point makes a difference of €60 a year. That is no reason to switch accounts every quarter. A comparison is worthwhile, however, if the rate for existing customers falls well below the deposit facility rate. The interest is capital income. At this order of magnitude it remains tax-free thanks to the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 a year. If the bank holds an exemption order (Freistellungsauftrag), it withholds no tax; otherwise the tax withheld can be reclaimed through your tax return.

- A separate instant-access savings account without a card, ideally at a different bank from your salary account. A transfer then takes a working day, which deliberately makes spontaneous withdrawals harder.
- Standing order at the start of the month, not at the end.
- Set interim targets: first €1,000, then three months, then the target size.
- After every withdrawal, topping the reserve back up takes priority over the monthly contribution to the portfolio.
- Adjust the reserve to current expenses once a year, because rent, children and where you live change the basis.

## Reasons against the portfolio

A common objection is that instant-access savings earn nothing in real terms, while a broadly diversified equity ETF has historically delivered much more. The money would therefore be lying idle in the instant-access account. The counter-argument is that the need for money and falling prices often have the same cause. In recessions, jobs are lost and prices fall at the same time. Short-time work (Kurzarbeit), slack order books and waves of layoffs often coincide with a market crash. A reserve held in the portfolio is therefore more likely to be needed precisely when it is worth least. Prices do, however, often recover sooner than the labour market. The DAX, for example, rose over the full year in both 2009 and 2020, although many employees were on short-time work in both years. The second reason is a practical one. A portfolio is designed for a long holding period, and regular withdrawals run counter to this purpose.

bloecke.titel: Example: the reserve in an ETF
bloecke.md: A reserve of €11,040 is held in an equity ETF. After a fall of 35%, €7,176 of it is left. The shortfall of €3,864 has to be financed some other way, through the arranged overdraft at an average of around 11.5% or through an instalment loan. At the same time, the entire holding is sold at the low. This realises the loss, and the later recovery takes place without this money. An instant-access savings account would have provided €11,040 at the same moment.

bloecke.titel: Cost of bridging €5,000 over twelve months
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation comparing the forgone instant-access interest at 2.0% with the cost of credit; the reserve is by far the cheapest option and the only one without a credit check.

bloecke.md:
## The cost of the reserve

These costs can be quantified. With 2.0% interest on instant-access savings and 3.3% inflation (the rate most recently reported, for September 2026), the buffer loses around 1.3% a year in real terms. On €12,000 that is about €150 of purchasing power a year and just over €1,400 over ten years. This is why the emergency fund should not be larger than necessary. But the same calculation also shows why a reserve is worthwhile at all. A loss of purchasing power of €1,400 over ten years is predictable. An arranged overdraft for the same €12,000 at 11.5%, by contrast, costs around €1,380 in a single year.

bloecke.titel: €12,000 in instant-access savings, nominal and in today's purchasing power
bloecke.unter: Illustrative calculation with 2.0% interest and 3.3% inflation. The balance rises while purchasing power falls, and the difference is the price of being able to access the money at any time.

bloecke.md:
- In the current account, the reserve is always visible and easily gets spent along with everything else. There is hardly any interest there anyway.
- Fixed-term deposits and notice accounts are unsuitable. With three months' notice, the money is available two months too late in an emergency.
- A reserve that is too large costs purchasing power. Beyond the target size for your own life situation, additional money hardly increases security any further.
- A buffer alongside an overdraft in use is expensive, because balances at 2% alongside debts at 11.5% cost the difference every day. A small residual buffer makes sense, and the rest pays off the overdraft.
- Holiday money and car savings belong in a different account. If they are mixed with the reserve, it will be empty in August.
- After a withdrawal, the reserve must be topped up again. An emptied emergency fund no longer protects you in the next emergency.

The basic rule of protection is to insure only risks that could ruin a household financially. Anything that can be paid from the reserve does not belong in an insurance policy. Households with several thousand euros of available reserve can choose higher excesses for contents, comprehensive car or legal expenses insurance and so permanently lower their premiums. They do not need mobile phone, glasses or travel luggage insurance. The emergency fund therefore pays off twice: when a claim arises and through lower premiums in every month before it.

mitnehmen: The size of the emergency fund depends on the expenses that continue in an emergency, not on net income or the full monthly budget.
Three to six months is usual; more with only one income, children, home ownership or self-employment, and less with two secure incomes.

The money belongs in a separate instant-access savings account covered by deposit protection, which is stable in nominal terms, available within a few working days and kept apart from the current account.
The reserve does not belong in the portfolio, because the need for money and falling prices typically have the same cause, and selling at the low makes the loss permanent.
The real loss in value of just over 1% a year is the price of this protection, so the reserve should be as large as necessary but no larger.

begriffe.text: A liquidity reserve worth several months of essential expenses, which is stable in nominal terms and must be available within a few working days. Its purpose is to avoid forced sales and expensive loans; returns are not the priority.
An interest-bearing bank account with no notice period and no price risk, which cannot be used for payments. The interest rate is variable and follows the central bank's deposit facility rate.
Statutory protection of bank balances up to €100,000 per customer and institution, which applies uniformly throughout the EU. Voluntary protection schemes of individual banking groups go further.

A benefit from statutory health insurance paid after six weeks of continued pay from the employer, for the same illness for a maximum of 72 weeks within three years. It replaces around 70% of gross pay, but at most 90% of net pay.
